title: Hooks, effects and data fetching
blurb: useEffect dependencies, cleanup, races, stale closures, custom hooks and the React 19 additions. Where most React interviews actually spend their time. Code assumes React 19 with createRoot and StrictMode off, unless the question says otherwise.

questions.q: What does the dependency array of `useEffect` actually control?
choices: Whether the component re-renders when any one of the listed values changes
The order in which the component's effects run relative to each other
Whether the effect re-runs after a render, comparing each value with `Object.is`
Which values the effect is allowed to read from the surrounding render
questions.why: The effect always runs after the first commit. On later renders React compares each dependency to its previous value and skips the effect if all match. Dependencies never cause a render; an empty array means 'never re-run' and no array means 'after every render'.
questions.asked: The foundation for every effect bug question that follows it.

questions.q: Why does this effect run after every render?
choices: A new object each render is a new reference, so the dependency changes
Objects cannot be dependencies, so React ignores the array entirely
The effect has no cleanup, so React re-runs it to be safe each time
`load` is not memoised, so the effect sees a new function every render
questions.why: `Object.is` compares references, and the object literal is recreated on every render. Depend on the primitive fields (`[options.page]`), build the object inside the effect, or memoise it. `load` is not in the array, so its identity is irrelevant here.
questions.asked: The infinite-loop bug everyone hits. It is really a JavaScript reference-equality question.

questions.q: An effect fetches results for `query`. A slow response for an old query arrives after the newest one. What is the standard fix?
choices: Remove the dependency array so the effect re-fetches after every render
Add a global lock so only one component in the app can fetch at a time
Ask the backend to guarantee that responses arrive in the order they were sent
Set a flag in the effect's cleanup and skip `setState` for stale responses
questions.why: Declare `let ignore = false` in the effect, check it before `setData`, and set `ignore = true` in the cleanup; cleanup runs before the next effect, so the stale response is discarded. `AbortController` also cancels the request itself. HTTP gives no ordering guarantee across requests.
questions.asked: The definitive React data-fetching question. Both fixes are acceptable; naming both is better.

questions.q: When does an effect's cleanup function run?
choices: Only when the component unmounts, never between re-runs
Before the effect re-runs, and once when it unmounts
After every render, whether or not the effect re-runs
Only when the component throws during rendering
questions.why: That ordering is what makes cleanup work for subscriptions: unsubscribe from the old id before subscribing to the new one. If the dependencies did not change, neither the effect nor its cleanup runs.
questions.asked: Getting this wrong is behind most leaked subscriptions and duplicated listeners.

questions.q: What is a stale closure in a hook?
choices: A hook that is called after its component has unmounted
A callback from an earlier render still reading that render's values
A `useMemo` cache that never invalidates when its inputs have changed
A ref whose `current` was read before it was first assigned
questions.why: Classic case: `setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000)` inside an effect with `[]` captures `count = 0` forever. Fix it with the updater `setCount(c => c + 1)` or a ref holding the latest value.
questions.asked: Very common, and it directly reuses the plain-JavaScript closure question.

questions.q: Which of these does NOT need an effect?
choices: Subscribing to a WebSocket for live updates
Adding a `keydown` listener to the document
Starting an interval timer for a countdown
Filtering a list by the current search input
questions.why: Filtering is a pure computation from existing state: do it during render, with `useMemo` only if it is genuinely expensive. Effects are for synchronising with systems outside React, which the other three all are.
questions.asked: 'You Might Not Need an Effect' is required reading, and interviewers know it.

questions.q: What is the difference between `useMemo` and `useCallback`?
choices: `useMemo` caches a computed value; `useCallback` caches a function itself
`useMemo` is for objects and arrays; `useCallback` is for primitive values
`useCallback` runs after the render commits; `useMemo` runs during render
`useCallback` memoises a component's output; `useMemo` memoises one value
questions.why: `useCallback(fn, deps)` is exactly `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`. Both keep a reference stable so a memoised child, or an effect dependency, does not see a change. Memoising a component's output is `memo`'s job.
questions.asked: The warm-up before 'and when would you actually use them?'.

questions.q: When does `React.memo` actually help?
choices: Always: wrapping every component is a free win in React 19
Only for components with no props, which can never need another update
When the component is costly and its props stay referentially stable
Whenever its parent re-renders often, whatever props it passes down
questions.why: `memo` does a shallow prop comparison. If the parent passes a new object or inline arrow every render, the comparison always fails and you have added cost for nothing. Fix the props, or colocate the state instead.
questions.asked: The wrong answer, 'wrap everything in memo', is a strong junior signal.

questions.q: What is `useRef` for, besides holding DOM nodes?
choices: Caching an expensive computation until its inputs change
Sharing a value between sibling components without props
Forcing a re-render whenever its `current` value is reassigned
Keeping a mutable value across renders without re-rendering
questions.why: Timer ids, the previous value of a prop, a 'has submitted' flag, the latest callback. Changing `ref.current` never re-renders, which is exactly why you must not read it during render to decide output. Caching a computation is `useMemo`.
questions.asked: It checks you know the difference between values that drive rendering and values that do not.

questions.q: What does this print on mount, inside `<StrictMode>` in development?
choices: run, clean, run
run, run, clean
run, clean
run (only once)
questions.why: In development StrictMode mounts, unmounts and remounts to prove your cleanup works. In production it logs 'run' once. If this double run breaks something, the effect is missing cleanup.
questions.asked: Everyone has googled 'why does my effect run twice'; the good answer knows it is deliberate.

questions.q: Which states does a fetched list screen need to render distinctly?
choices: Loading and loaded, since an error just shows the loaded view
Loading, error, empty, and loaded with data
Pending and settled, matching the promise states
Idle, running and done, as a task runner would
questions.why: Empty is the one people forget, and it ships a blank screen with no explanation. Error needs its own view with a retry. A discriminated union makes the states explicit and impossible to conflate; some screens add an `idle` state before the first request.
questions.asked: A practical question about whether you have shipped a real screen.

questions.q: Why is this custom hook wrong?
choices: The early return makes `useState` conditional, breaking call order
Custom hooks cannot return `null`; they must return an array
`useState` must be given a function, not a value, inside a hook
The hook is fine; only the component calling it must be unconditional
questions.why: Hooks are matched by call position. With `attempts` in slot 1, the first render with a truthy `id` calls a second hook React has no record of and throws 'Rendered more hooks than during the previous render'. Had the conditional hook been the only one, React would silently treat each 0-to-1 change as a fresh mount and drop the state instead. Move every hook above any conditional return; the rule applies inside custom hooks too.
questions.asked: It checks that the rules of hooks are understood as a mechanism, including inside custom hooks.

questions.q: When should you extract a custom hook?
choices: Whenever a component grows beyond about fifty lines of code
When two components need to render the same piece of markup
When state-plus-effect logic repeats or obscures the component
When two components must share one and the same live state instance
questions.why: A custom hook shares logic, not state: two components using `useFetch` each get their own copy. Shared markup is a component, and shared live state needs lifting or context.
questions.asked: 'Have you written a custom hook?' is a standard mid-level filter.

questions.q: How do you read the latest value inside a `setInterval` started once on mount?
choices: Keep the latest value in a ref and read `ref.current` inside the callback
Add the value to the effect's dependencies so the callback always sees it
Wrap the value in `useMemo` so the interval callback reads a stable copy
Store the value in state and read it back from the setter's return value
questions.why: Adding it to the dependencies tears down and recreates the interval on every change, which resets its timing. A ref keeps the interval alive while giving the callback a live view; in React 19.2 `useEffectEvent` is the built-in form of the same idea. Setters return nothing. This is the standard `useInterval` pattern.
questions.asked: It tests whether you can fix a stale closure without breaking the timer.

questions.q: What does `useLayoutEffect` do differently from `useEffect`?
choices: It runs before the component renders, so it can prepare the state
It runs only on the server, during streaming server rendering
It runs after paint like `useEffect`, but with no dependencies
It runs after DOM changes but before the browser paints them
questions.why: Use it when you must measure or adjust the DOM before the user sees a flash: a tooltip's position, a scroll restore. It blocks paint, so it is the exception, not the default. On the server it does not run at all.
questions.asked: The flicker-before-paint scenario shows whether you understand when effects run relative to the screen.

questions.q: What does the exhaustive-deps lint rule report here, and is it right?
choices: Nothing: an empty array correctly means 'run once on mount'
`userId` is missing, and yes: the effect keeps the first id
`loadUser` is missing, but `userId` can safely be left out
It asks for the array to be removed so the effect always runs
questions.why: An empty array claims the captured values are correct forever. When `userId` changes the effect never re-runs and the screen shows the wrong user. `loadUser` is a module import, not a render value, so it does not belong in the array.
questions.asked: The follow-up: 'when is it legitimate to omit a dependency?' Essentially never; restructure instead.

questions.q: How do you stop a search box's effect firing one request per keystroke?
choices: Wrap the change handler in `useCallback` so it is created only once
Schedule it with `setTimeout` in the effect and clear it in cleanup
Make the effect `async` and `await` a 300 ms sleep before fetching
Throttle the component's rendering so it re-renders less often
questions.why: `const t = setTimeout(() => search(q), 300); return () => clearTimeout(t);` cancels the pending request on every keystroke, so only a pause fires one; a `useDebouncedValue` hook is the same idea. The async sleep cancels nothing, so every keystroke still fires, just later.
questions.asked: It checks you can use effect cleanup as a cancellation tool, not only for unsubscribing.

questions.q: When do you need the updater form `setX(prev => next)`?
choices: When you need the update to apply synchronously before the next line
Only inside `useReducer`, where the reducer receives the previous state
When the state is an object, because objects are always compared by reference
When the next value depends on the previous and the closure may be stale
questions.why: React passes the latest queued state to the updater, so it is correct inside intervals, repeated calls in one handler, and async callbacks. It does not make the update synchronous. It also lets you drop the state from an effect's dependency array.
questions.asked: It links stale closures to the everyday fix, which interviewers expect you to reach for first.

questions.q: In a modern React app, where should most data fetching live?
choices: In a data layer, such as a query library or router loaders
In `useEffect` inside each component that displays the data
In the render body, so the data is ready before the JSX
In a global variable that is populated once at startup
questions.why: Hand-rolled effects re-solve caching, deduplication, retries, races and invalidation every time. Knowing how to write the effect by hand matters; knowing why teams do not matters just as much. Fetching in the render body re-fires on every render.
questions.asked: The strong answer names the concerns a data library handles for you.

questions.q: What happens if a component calls `setState` unconditionally during render?
choices: It is queued and applied on the next event the user triggers
It throws immediately, because setters are disabled in render
React re-renders at once, looping until 'Too many re-renders'
It is ignored, because React discards updates made while rendering
questions.why: React re-runs the component straight away with the new state, which calls the setter again, until it gives up with 'Too many re-renders'. There is one legitimate use, adjusting state when a prop changes behind a comparison guard, but it is rare.
questions.asked: The 'Too many re-renders' error is common; this checks you can explain it.

questions.q: Why might a `useMemo`'d prop not stop a child from re-rendering?
choices: `useMemo` only works on primitives, so an object is recreated anyway
`useMemo` needs an empty dependency array to keep its value stable
Memoised values are recomputed on every render in development builds
The child is not wrapped in `memo`, so it renders with its parent
questions.why: Stabilising a prop only matters to something that compares props. Without `memo` the child re-renders whenever its parent does, so you have paid for the memo and got nothing.
questions.asked: It separates people who memoise by habit from people who know what the memo is for.

questions.q: What does `useSyncExternalStore` solve?
choices: Persisting component state to `localStorage` between page reloads
Making effects run synchronously after the DOM has been updated
Reading an outside store so renders stay consistent under concurrency
Keeping state in sync across browser tabs through a broadcast channel
questions.why: Subscribing by hand with `useEffect` can tear: different components render from different versions of the store in one pass. This hook is the supported way to bridge an external store such as a state library or a browser API.
questions.asked: It shows whether you know how state libraries integrate with React, not just how to call them.

questions.q: Your effect sets state, which changes a dependency, which re-runs the effect. What is the fix?
choices: Add a ref guard so the effect body runs only the first time
Break the loop: derive the value, or depend on a primitive
Remove the dependency array so React stops comparing values
Wrap the `setState` call in `setTimeout` to defer the update
questions.why: A guard hides the symptom and leaves a component that works by accident. The real question is why the value is in state at all; usually it should be computed during render. Removing the array makes it run after every render, which is worse.
questions.asked: A debugging scenario: the good answer diagnoses rather than patches.

questions.q: What does an error boundary catch?
choices: Errors thrown while rendering the tree below it
Every error in the app, including rejected promises
Errors thrown inside event handlers below it
Failed network requests made by its children
questions.why: It catches errors during rendering, lifecycle methods and constructors of its subtree. It does not catch errors in event handlers, async code or itself; those need ordinary try/catch. Without one, a render error unmounts the whole app.
questions.asked: The follow-up, 'what about an error in onClick?', catches people who think boundaries catch everything.

questions.q: In React 19, what does wrapping `setTab(next)` in `startTransition` change?
choices: The update runs on a worker thread, so its rendering never blocks the page
The update is delayed by a fixed timeout, like a built-in debounce
The update is non-urgent, so React can interrupt it to handle input first
The update skips reconciliation and replaces the DOM subtree directly
questions.why: A transition marks a state update as interruptible: urgent updates such as typing render first, and `isPending` from `useTransition` lets you show that work is in progress. It is still ordinary rendering on the main thread, with no fixed delay.
questions.asked: It checks whether 'concurrent React' means anything concrete to you beyond the buzzword.

questions.q: In React 19, a slow list is rendered with `useDeferredValue(query)`. What happens as the user types?
choices: The input updates at once; the list catches up, showing old results meanwhile
The input waits until the list has finished rendering each new query
The list renders only after the user stops typing for a fixed delay
The list renders on a background thread while the input stays fully responsive
questions.why: React renders urgently with the old deferred value, then tries a background render with the new one and abandons it if more typing arrives. Unlike a debounce there is no fixed delay: on a fast device the list keeps up immediately.
questions.asked: Comparing it to a debounce is the follow-up; the no-fixed-delay point is what a strong answer adds.

questions.q: What is `useId` for?
choices: Generating stable `key` values for items in a rendered list
Generating ids for new database records created by a form
Reading the DOM `id` of the root element that the component rendered
Generating unique ids for accessibility attributes like `htmlFor`
questions.why: It returns an id unique to the component instance and identical on server and client, so `<label htmlFor={id}>` and `<input id={id}>` match after hydration. List keys must come from your data, and it knows nothing about databases.
questions.asked: It checks you know the hook exists before you hand-roll counters that break server rendering.

questions.q: What does the arrow function change in the second line?
questions.code:
useState(readDraft());       // A
useState(() => readDraft()); // B
choices: B reads the draft lazily, on the first click instead of on mount
B calls `readDraft` only on the first render; A calls it every render
B stores the function itself as the state instead of its result
Nothing: React calls `readDraft` only once in both of the forms
questions.why: The argument to `useState` is used only on the first render, but in form A the call `readDraft()` still executes on every render, wasting work such as parsing `localStorage`. Passing a function lets React call it once.
questions.asked: A small optimisation that shows you know what runs on every render.

questions.q: Why is `useEffect(async () => { ... }, [id])` a mistake?
choices: Async functions run on another thread, so their `setState` calls are lost
An effect must return nothing or a cleanup, and an async function returns a promise
React waits for the promise, which blocks rendering until the fetch finishes
Effects cannot call `fetch`; data loading must happen in event handlers
questions.why: React treats the effect's return value as its cleanup, and a promise is not a function, so React warns and cleanup is impossible. Define an async function inside the effect and call it, keeping the cleanup (such as an ignore flag) synchronous.
questions.asked: A very common first attempt at fetching, so it checks the effect contract is understood.

questions.q: In React 19, how does a function component receive a `ref` its parent passes?
choices: Only by wrapping the component in `forwardRef` first
Through `useRef`, which returns the parent's ref
Through context, set up by the parent's provider
As an ordinary prop called `ref`, with no wrapper
questions.why: From React 19, `ref` is a regular prop for function components, so `function Input({ ref, ...props })` works and `forwardRef` is no longer needed (it still works, and is slated for deprecation). `useRef` creates a new ref; it does not receive one.
questions.asked: It checks whether your React knowledge is current, since forwardRef boilerplate is in most older code.

questions.q: What does `useImperativeHandle` let a component do?
choices: Expose a custom object, such as `{ focus }`, to its parent's ref
Run an effect before the browser paints, like `useLayoutEffect`
Call a parent's methods directly, without passing any callbacks down
Force a synchronous re-render from outside the component tree
questions.why: Instead of handing the parent the raw DOM node, the child exposes a narrow API (`focus()`, `scrollToRow(n)`), keeping its internals private. It is an escape hatch for imperative actions; data should still flow through props.
questions.asked: It comes up when designing reusable inputs or tables, and tests restraint with escape hatches.

questions.q: In React 19, when does the function returned from this ref callback run?
questions.code:
<div ref={(node) => {
  observer.observe(node);
  return () => observer.unobserve(node);
}} />
choices: Never: React ignores the return value of ref callbacks
Only when the `observer` object itself is garbage collected
When the ref detaches: on unmount, or when the callback changes
After every render, whether or not the element was replaced
questions.why: React 19 added cleanup functions to ref callbacks: React calls the cleanup when detaching instead of calling the ref with `null`. An inline arrow is a new function each render, so it detaches and re-attaches on every re-render; hoist or memoise it if that matters.
questions.asked: It checks current React knowledge and whether you notice the inline-callback re-attach cost.

questions.q: In React 19.2, what problem does `useEffectEvent` solve?
choices: Letting event handlers run inside effects, so that clicks can be simulated
Letting an effect run only once, even in StrictMode development builds
Letting an effect subscribe to DOM events without adding a cleanup
Letting an effect read the latest props without re-running when they change
questions.why: A function from `useEffectEvent` always sees the latest render's values but is not a dependency, so a chat effect can log with the current `theme` without reconnecting when `theme` changes. Call it only from inside effects. It replaces the 'latest value in a ref' workaround.
questions.asked: It shows you know the current answer to the oldest dependency-array complaint.

questions.q: Why does the lint rule not ask you to list `setCount` in an effect's dependencies?
choices: Setters may only be called in handlers, so effects never use them
Setters are recreated each render, but React ignores their changes
React keeps a state setter's identity stable across all renders
Dependencies may only hold state values, never any function values
questions.why: `useState` setters and `useReducer`'s `dispatch` are the same function for the component's whole life, so listing them changes nothing. Other functions defined in the component are new each render and do belong in the array.
questions.asked: It checks you know which values are stable, which is the basis of reading any dependency array.

questions.q: Can you rely on `useMemo` to run its function only once for a given set of dependencies?
choices: Yes: React guarantees the cached value lives as long as the component
No: it is a performance hint, and React may discard the cache and recompute
Yes, provided the dependency values are all primitives rather than objects
No: it recomputes on every render in production and only caches in development
questions.why: The docs describe `useMemo` as an optimisation: React may throw the cached value away (for example for offscreen components) and call your function again. Code must stay correct if that happens; for a value that must persist, use state or a ref.
questions.asked: It catches code that uses `useMemo` for correctness, such as creating a single connection.

questions.q: In what order do these effects log on mount?
choices: child, parent
parent, child
child only
parent only
questions.why: Rendering goes top-down (Parent renders before Child), but effects run bottom-up after commit, so children's effects fire first. That is why a parent's effect can safely rely on refs and DOM set up by its children.
questions.asked: It separates people who have debugged effect ordering from people who assume top-down everywhere.

questions.q: In React 19, a component calls `use(promise)` and the promise is still pending. What happens?
choices: `use` returns `undefined`, and the component renders again on resolve
React blocks the main thread until the promise resolves, then renders
The component suspends, and the nearest `<Suspense>` shows its fallback
React throws an error unless the call is wrapped in `try`/`catch`
questions.why: `use` suspends the component; the closest `<Suspense>` boundary renders its fallback and React retries when the promise settles. A rejection goes to the nearest error boundary. The promise should come from a cache or a parent, not be created during render.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know how Suspense-based data loading actually works in React 19.

questions.q: An error boundary shows its fallback after a crash on user 1. The user opens user 2 and still sees the fallback. What is the simplest fix?
choices: Render the boundary with `key={userId}` so it remounts per user
Call `setState` in an effect to clear the error when the user changes
Add a Retry button to the fallback that re-renders its parent
Wrap the user component in `memo` so it re-renders for new users
questions.why: An error boundary keeps its error state until it remounts, and a new `key` forces exactly that. Re-rendering the parent passes new props but keeps the boundary's error state, and `memo` does not reset state either.
questions.asked: It combines two ideas, key-based reset and boundary state, which is what real debugging needs.

questions.q: What is the difference between these two lines?
questions.code:
const [rows, setRows] = useState(parseCsv(text));
const [rows, setRows] = useState(() => parseCsv(text));
choices: None; React only calls the initial value once either way
The second re-parses whenever `text` changes after mount
The first is memoised by React; the second is recomputed each time
The first parses on every render; the second only on mount
questions.why: Arguments are evaluated before `useState` is called, so the first line runs `parseCsv` every render and throws the result away after mount. Passing a function (a lazy initialiser) makes React call it only for the initial state. Neither version reacts to later `text` changes.
questions.asked: Simple, but checks that you know how JavaScript evaluates arguments.

questions.q: `Editor` does `const [name, setName] = useState(initialName)`. The parent later passes a different `initialName`. What does the input show?
choices: The new `initialName`, because the prop it came from changed
An empty string until the user types in it again
The old value: the initial state is read only on mount
The new value, but only in development builds
questions.why: The argument to `useState` is used only for the first render; later values are ignored. If the editor should restart for a new record, give it `key={record.id}`. Syncing the prop into state with an effect is the usual wrong fix.
questions.asked: The "my state does not update when the prop changes" bug, from the other side.

questions.q: `count` is 0. The user clicks "Show later", then clicks "+1" twice within three seconds. What does the alert show?
choices: 0, the value in the render that made the handler
2, the latest value when the timer fires
1, because only one update had rendered
It depends on whether React batched the two clicks together
questions.why: Each render has its own `count`, and the timeout callback closes over the one from the render where it was created. State is a snapshot, not a live variable. If you need the latest value in delayed code, read it from a ref.
questions.asked: Tests the state-as-snapshot model with timers, a common interview scenario.

questions.q: In development with `<StrictMode>`, this `addItem` sometimes adds the item twice. Why?
choices: StrictMode dispatches every click event twice in development builds
The spread copies the array twice, which duplicates the new item
StrictMode calls updater functions twice, and this one mutates `prev`
React queues the update once per render of the parent component tree
questions.why: Updaters must be pure. In development StrictMode may call them twice with the same `prev`; since this one mutates `prev`, the second call pushes again. `return [...prev, item]` is safe under any number of calls. Events are never dispatched twice.
questions.asked: Shows you understand what StrictMode's double calls are designed to catch.

questions.q: In development with `<StrictMode>`, how many times does `"init"` log when this component mounts?
choices: Once, because lazy initialisers are exempt
Twice, since initialisers are double-called too
Three times, once per StrictMode check
Never, because lazy initialisers run before render starts
questions.why: StrictMode double-invokes component bodies, lazy initialisers, updaters and reducers in development so impure logic shows up. One result is discarded. In production it logs once; do not do side effects inside initialisers.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know exactly which functions StrictMode double-calls.

questions.q: `id` goes from 1 to 2. What does this log, in order, for that change?
choices: `setup 2`, then `cleanup 1`
`cleanup 2`, then `setup 2`
`setup 2` only; cleanup waits for unmount
`cleanup 1`, then `setup 2`
questions.why: Before re-running an effect, React runs the previous cleanup, and that cleanup closes over the old render's `id`. So you always see the old value torn down before the new one is set up. Cleanup runs on every re-run, not only on unmount.
questions.asked: Checks the setup/cleanup rhythm that every subscription depends on.

questions.q: The same effect ran with `id` 1, then 2. The component now unmounts. What does the cleanup log?
choices: `cleanup 2`, the last committed id
`cleanup 1`, the first render's id
`cleanup undefined`, props are gone
Nothing, cleanup was already used
questions.why: Each cleanup belongs to the effect run that created it. The live effect is the one from `id` 2, so unmount runs its cleanup with 2. The cleanup for 1 already ran when `id` changed.
questions.asked: Tests that each render's effect and cleanup are paired.

questions.q: How many times does this component render on mount (StrictMode off)?
questions.code:
const [ready, setReady] = useState(false);
useEffect(() => setReady(true), []);
choices: Once, because the effect runs before paint
Three times, due to the dependency check
Once, since setting state in an effect is batched away
Twice: mount, then again for the new state
questions.why: Effects run after the first render is committed, and setting state there schedules a second render. If `ready` could be computed during render, do that instead and save a render (and a flash of the `false` UI).
questions.asked: Why "setState in an effect" costs a render is basic but often misunderstood.

questions.q: Which of these is a good use of `useEffect`?
choices: Filtering a list when the search text changes
Keeping `document.title` in step with an `unread` count
Sending a POST request right after the user clicks Save
Resetting a form's fields whenever `userId` changes
questions.why: `document.title` is an external system that must stay in sync with state, which is exactly what effects are for. Filtering is derived during render, a POST belongs in the click handler, and resetting state on a prop change is a job for `key`.
questions.asked: The "you might not need an effect" test from the positive side.

questions.q: What goes wrong with this effect as `delay` changes over time?
choices: Nothing; the browser dedupes listeners for the same event
Nothing, as long as `onScroll` is wrapped in `useCallback`
React removes the old listener itself when `delay` changes
Every run adds another listener, and none are ever removed
questions.why: Without a cleanup that calls `removeEventListener`, each effect run stacks a new listener and they outlive the component. The browser only dedupes the exact same function reference, which `onScroll` usually is not across renders. React knows nothing about listeners you add.
questions.asked: Missing cleanup is the most common effect bug in code reviews.

questions.q: Why does this cleanup fail to remove the resize listener?
choices: The cleanup passes a new function, not the one that was added
Cleanups cannot touch `window` after the component unmounts
Resize listeners need `{ passive: true }` to be removable
The empty dependency array stops the cleanup from ever running
questions.why: `removeEventListener` matches by function reference, and two identical-looking arrows are different objects. Store the handler in a variable inside the effect and pass the same one to both calls. Cleanups with `[]` do run, on unmount.
questions.asked: Checks you know how listener removal matches handlers.

questions.q: The effect's cleanup calls `controller.abort()`. The user navigates away mid-request. What does the `.catch` do?
questions.code:
fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal })
  .then((r) => r.json())
  .then(setData)
  .catch((e) => setError(e.message));
choices: Nothing: an aborted fetch resolves with an empty body
Nothing: aborted promises never settle, so it never runs
It throws an uncaught error because the component is gone
It sets an "aborted" error, so filter out `AbortError`
questions.why: Aborting rejects the fetch promise with a `DOMException` named `AbortError`, so a blanket `catch` treats your own cancellation as a failure. Check `e.name === "AbortError"` (or `signal.aborted`) and ignore it. Setting state after unmount is a silent no-op.
questions.asked: Cancelling correctly means also handling the cancellation you caused.

questions.q: An effect uses an `ignore` flag set to `true` in cleanup, so late responses are dropped. What does the flag not do?
choices: Stop a stale response from overwriting newer data
Cancel the HTTP request, which still uses bandwidth
Prevent state updates after the component unmounts
Work correctly with StrictMode's setup-cleanup-setup run
questions.why: The flag only stops you from using a result; the request still runs to completion on the network and the server. `AbortController` actually cancels it. The flag does handle races, unmounts and StrictMode's setup-cleanup-setup correctly.
questions.asked: Tells apart "ignore the answer" from "cancel the request"; both are valid tools.

questions.q: Why does this effect run after every render, even when `query` has not changed?
choices: `params` is a new object each render, so `Object.is` sees a change
Effects compare objects deeply, and `page` is a number literal
An object dependency disables dependency checks entirely
`search` is missing from the array, so React re-runs it every time to be safe
questions.why: Dependencies are compared with `Object.is`, so a freshly created object is always "different". Create the object inside the effect and depend on `query`, or memoise it. React never deep-compares, and missing deps do not change when it runs.
questions.asked: The core reason for re-running effects; interviewers expect `Object.is` by name.

questions.q: `load` is declared in the component body and used by an effect. Listing `[load]` makes the effect run every render. What is usually the cleanest fix?
choices: Remove `load` from the array and silence the lint rule
Store `load` in a ref and depend on `loadRef` instead
Move `load` inside the effect and depend on what it reads
Wrap the whole effect body in `useMemo` with an empty array
questions.why: A function declared in the body is a new object each render. If only the effect uses it, move it inside so the dependencies become the values it reads, such as `userId`. `useCallback` also works when the function is shared; lying to the linter creates stale data.
questions.asked: Shows the preferred order of fixes for function dependencies.

questions.q: A parent re-creates `user` as a new object on every render, with the same data. Which dependency list stops the fetch re-running needlessly?
choices: `[user]`
`[JSON.stringify(user)]`
`[user.id]`
questions.why: Depend on the primitive the effect actually reads: `user.id` compares by value. `[user]` changes identity every render, stringifying works but costs work and re-runs on unrelated field changes, and `[]` never refetches for a different user.
questions.asked: Tests narrowing dependencies to what the effect reads.

questions.q: This profile screen shows the first user forever, even after `userId` changes. Why?
choices: `setUser` is stale, so later responses are ignored by React
Effects never re-run for prop changes, only for state changes
The empty array runs the effect only on mount, so it never refetches
The promise is cached by React, so later calls return the first user
questions.why: The effect reads `userId` but does not list it, so React has no reason to re-run it. Add `[userId]` (the exhaustive-deps lint rule would flag this). Props and state are treated the same as dependencies, and setters are stable.
questions.asked: The most common dependency bug; the lint rule is the expected mention.

questions.q: A `Toggle` keeps `on` in state and uses an effect to call `onChange(on)` whenever `on` changes. What is the better design?
choices: Call `onChange(next)` in the click handler, next to `setOn(next)`
Keep it, but add `onChange` to the effect's dependency array
Move the effect into a `useLayoutEffect` so the parent updates first
Wrap `onChange` in `useCallback` inside the Toggle itself
questions.why: Notifying the parent is a response to a user event, not synchronisation. Calling it in the handler updates both in one batched render; the effect adds a render pass and fires on mount too. Better still, lift the state up and make `Toggle` controlled.
questions.asked: Checks the events-versus-effects distinction on a realistic component.

questions.q: A form sets `submitted` to `true` on click, and an effect on `[submitted]` sends the POST. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing, effects are the right place for network requests
It should be a `useLayoutEffect`, or the POST can be lost on a fast navigation
The flag must be a ref, or the effect runs twice per click
The POST belongs in the submit handler; the effect adds a delay and fragility
questions.why: Sending a form is caused by a specific interaction, so it belongs in that event handler. The flag-plus-effect version adds a render, can re-send when the flag is re-set or on remount, and hides the cause. Effects are for syncing with what is on screen.
questions.asked: Tests the React docs rule of thumb: why is this code running?

questions.q: In development, a page-view analytics effect logs two page views on mount. What should you do?
choices: Guard it with a `useRef` flag so the call only ever runs a single time
Nothing: it is StrictMode's dev-only re-run; production sends one
Move the call to `useLayoutEffect`, which is not double-run
Turn off StrictMode, since it breaks analytics everywhere
questions.why: StrictMode mounts, unmounts and remounts in development to test cleanups; production runs the effect once per mount. For analytics the duplicate is harmless (or filter dev traffic). Ref guards hide real cleanup bugs, and layout effects are re-run too.
questions.asked: Checks you will not "fix" StrictMode by fighting it.

questions.q: App start-up must run `initAuth()` exactly once per page load, even in StrictMode development. What does the React documentation suggest?
choices: An effect with `[]`, which production and dev run once
A `useRef(false)` flag set on first run in the root component
A module-level `let didInit` flag checked inside the effect
Calling `initAuth()` directly in the root component body
questions.why: Truly once-per-app logic is not tied to a component's mount, so guard it at module level (or run it before `createRoot`). A ref resets when the component remounts, the effect re-runs in dev, and the component body can run many times.
questions.asked: Separates "once per mount" from "once per app", which people often conflate.

questions.q: Why does this effect not re-run when a different element is later stored in `boxRef.current`?
choices: Refs are frozen after the first commit, so the value never changes
`boxRef.current` is compared deeply, and two DOM nodes always compare as equal
React strips `.current` expressions out of dependency arrays
Mutating a ref does not cause a render, so the new value is never checked
questions.why: Dependencies are only compared when the component renders, and writing `ref.current` never schedules one. To react to a node appearing or changing, use a ref callback. Refs are ordinary mutable objects; nothing freezes them.
questions.asked: The lint rule warns about this; knowing why shows you understand refs.

questions.q: With server-side rendering, which of these runs on the server?
choices: `useEffect` callbacks, which run before the HTML is streamed out
Only `useLayoutEffect`, because it is synchronous
Everything, then again during hydration on the client
The component body, but not `useEffect` or `useLayoutEffect`
questions.why: Server rendering only calls components to produce HTML; effects run after commit, and there is no commit on the server. That is why browser APIs such as `localStorage` belong in effects or event handlers, not in the render body.
questions.asked: Explains a whole class of "window is not defined" errors.

questions.q: A list screen fetches on mount. Which initial state avoids a brief "No results" flash?
questions.code:
const [rows, setRows] = useState([]);
const [loading, setLoading] = useState(/* ? */);
choices: `true`, set to `false` once the request settles
`false`, then set it to `true` inside the effect
`null`, meaning unknown until the effect runs
`undefined`, so React skips the first render
questions.why: The first render happens before any effect, so starting at `false` with empty rows renders the empty state for one frame. Start `true` (or better, model `status: "loading"`). React never skips renders for `undefined`.
questions.asked: Small detail that shows care about loading states.

questions.q: In development with StrictMode, the Network tab shows the first request of this screen marked "cancelled", then a second identical request. Why?
choices: The browser retried a failed request, which is a normal network event
StrictMode re-ran the effect; its cleanup aborted the first fetch
React deduped the two requests and cancelled the slower one
The dev server restarted, and the page loaded twice in a row
questions.why: StrictMode runs setup, cleanup, setup on mount in development. A cleanup that calls `abort()` cancels the first request, which proves the cleanup works. In production only one request is made. React has no request deduplication of its own.
questions.asked: A real "is this a bug?" moment; the confident answer explains the dev behaviour.

questions.q: Which of these is a legitimate effect?
choices: Recomputing `total` from `items` into another state variable
Calling `setPage(1)` whenever the filter text changes
Showing a toast after the Save button's request succeeds
Writing `settings` to `localStorage` whenever it changes
questions.why: Local storage is an external system to keep in step with state, so an effect on `[settings]` fits. `total` is derived data, resetting the page belongs where the filter is changed, and the toast is part of the save handler's result.
questions.asked: Recognising legitimate effects matters as much as avoiding the wrong ones.

questions.q: A chat effect connects to `roomId` and its cleanup disconnects. The user switches from room "a" to room "b". What happens?
choices: It connects to "b" and stays connected to "a" too
It connects to "b", then disconnects from "a"
It disconnects from "a", then connects to "b"
Nothing, until the component unmounts and remounts
questions.why: When a dependency changes React runs the old cleanup (disconnect "a") before the new setup (connect "b"). The effect describes how to sync with one room; React handles switching. Without the cleanup you would leak connections.
questions.asked: The canonical example of thinking in synchronisation, not lifecycle.

questions.q: A teammate uses `[JSON.stringify(filters)]` as an effect's dependency list. What is the trade-off?
choices: It re-runs only when the content changes, but serialises every render
It is exactly as cheap as listing `filters` itself
It breaks the effect, because arrays cannot hold strings
It re-runs on every render, because the string is a brand new value each time
questions.why: Strings compare by value, so the effect runs only when the serialised content changes, but you pay to stringify on every render and key order matters. Often it is cleaner to depend on the few primitive fields the effect uses, or keep `filters` stable at the source.
questions.asked: A pragmatic hack; the strong answer names both its cost and the cleaner fix.

questions.q: A tooltip reads its anchor's `getBoundingClientRect()` in `useEffect` and sets its position. Users see it flash at the wrong place first. What is the fix?
choices: Measure in the render body instead of in an effect
Wrap the position update in `startTransition` so it is not urgent
Add a `setTimeout(0)` before measuring the element
Use `useLayoutEffect`, which runs before the browser paints
questions.why: `useEffect` usually runs after paint, so the first frame shows the default position. `useLayoutEffect` runs after DOM mutations but before paint, and a state update inside it re-renders synchronously, so users only see the final position. The DOM does not exist yet during render.
questions.asked: The textbook case for `useLayoutEffect`; say why it blocks paint.

questions.q: Who is `useInsertionEffect` meant for?
choices: Any component that needs to insert extra DOM nodes after it renders
CSS-in-JS libraries that must inject styles before layout effects read them
Portals, which must insert their container into the body before mounting
List components that insert rows at a given index
questions.why: It fires before any layout effects so a styling library can add `<style>` rules that layout code will then measure correctly. It cannot update state or read refs. Application code almost never needs it.
questions.asked: Knowing it exists and that you should not use it is the whole answer.

questions.q: What does this counter show after five seconds?
choices: 5, one increment per second
0, the interval never fires
1, and it stays there
It climbs by 2 per second
questions.why: The interval callback was created in the first render and closes over `count = 0`, so every tick sets the count to `0 + 1`. After the first tick the value no longer changes and React bails out. The fix is the updater `setCount((c) => c + 1)`.
questions.asked: The canonical stale-closure example; you should both predict it and fix it.

questions.q: `n` is set to 5 after mount. The user then presses a key. What does this log?
choices: `n is 5`, the current value of the state variable
`n is 0`, the value when the listener was added
`n is undefined`, since the effect has ended
Nothing: the listener was removed on re-render
questions.why: The listener was created once, in the effect from the first render, so it sees that render's `n`. With `[]` it is never replaced. Add `n` to the dependencies so the listener is re-attached, or read the latest value through a ref or `useEffectEvent`.
questions.asked: Global listeners are where stale closures hit real apps.

questions.q: Which change fixes the stuck counter without restarting the interval?
choices: Use `setCount((c) => c + 1)` in the callback
Add `count` to the dependency array
Declare `count` with `let` instead of `const`
Move `setInterval` into `useLayoutEffect`
questions.why: The updater receives the latest state from React, so the callback no longer needs `count` at all and the effect can keep `[]`. Adding `count` to the deps also works but tears down and recreates the interval every tick.
questions.asked: Tests the simplest correct fix and awareness of the alternative's cost.

questions.q: A polling effect lists `[count]` so the callback sees the latest value. What is the side effect of that fix?
choices: The callback still sees the first `count`, because intervals capture once
React throws a warning, since interval ids cannot change between renders
Nothing changes, because dependency arrays are ignored for timer-based effects
The interval is cleared and recreated on every change, resetting its timing
questions.why: Each change runs the cleanup and starts a fresh interval, so the timer restarts from zero; with frequent changes it may never fire. The updater form, a ref, or `useEffectEvent` avoid the restart. After each re-run the callback does see the fresh value, so staleness is no longer the problem.
questions.asked: Shows you think about the behaviour of the fix, not just the lint rule.

questions.q: A long-lived callback must always read the latest `onMessage` prop without re-subscribing. What is the classic pre-19.2 pattern?
choices: Put `onMessage` in state and always read it through the updater form of the setter
Keep it in a ref updated in an effect, and call `ref.current()` from the callback
Wrap `onMessage` in `useMemo` with an empty dependency array so it never goes stale
Pass `onMessage` to the subscription on every render instead
questions.why: A ref is a mutable box the callback can read at call time; updating `ref.current = onMessage` in an effect keeps it current without re-running the subscription. `useMemo([])` freezes the first function. React 19.2's `useEffectEvent` packages this pattern officially.
questions.asked: The "latest ref" pattern is common in library code and custom hooks.

questions.q: Why does `save` always send the first value of `draft`?
choices: `useCallback` copies `draft` by value when it is called
`api.save` caches its first argument and ignores later ones
The empty deps keep the first function, which closed over the first `draft`
State values are frozen inside callbacks passed to `useCallback`, by design, for safety
questions.why: `useCallback` returns the same function until a dependency changes, and that function closes over the render it came from. List `draft` in the deps, or read it from a ref if identity must stay fixed. Nothing is frozen; the function simply never updates.
questions.asked: Stale memoised callbacks are a common side effect of over-using `useCallback`.

questions.q: After `await api.remove(id)`, this handler checks `items.length` to decide whether to show the empty state. Why is the check wrong?
choices: `items` becomes `undefined` after an `await` inside a React event handler
The `await` makes React re-run the whole handler with the new `items` array
`setItems` has not been called yet when the `await` begins
`items` is this render's snapshot, so it still includes the deleted row
questions.why: State does not change inside a running function; `items` is the value from the render that created the handler. Compute the next array once, pass it to `setItems`, and use that same variable for the check. Derived UI such as the empty state is better rendered from state anyway.
questions.asked: Async handlers mixed with state are where the snapshot model trips people up.

questions.q: What does the button show after it is clicked twice?
choices: It throws, refs are read-only in JSX
questions.why: Changing `ref.current` does not schedule a render, so the JSX still shows the value from the last render, 0. Use state for anything the screen shows. Refs are for values that must survive renders without causing them.
questions.asked: The first thing to know about refs versus state.

questions.q: A component starts a `setTimeout` in a click handler and must cancel it in another handler. Where should the timer id live?
choices: In a local `let` variable declared in the component body
In state, so React knows a timer is currently running
In a `useRef`, which keeps the same box across renders
In a module-level variable shared by all instances
questions.why: A ref survives re-renders and changing it does not cause one, which fits a value nothing renders. A local variable is re-declared every render, state adds pointless renders, and a module variable is shared by every instance of the component.
questions.asked: Checks you choose refs for exactly the right kind of value.

questions.q: What does this log on the first render?
choices: The `<input>` element
`undefined`
An empty object
`null`
questions.why: React sets DOM refs during the commit phase, after rendering. On the first render the element does not exist yet, so `current` still holds the initial `null`. Read DOM refs in effects or event handlers.
questions.asked: Tests understanding of when refs are attached.

questions.q: A search page should focus its input when it first appears. Which is a correct approach?
choices: Call it in `useEffect(() => ..., [])`, or use `autoFocus`
Call `inputRef.current.focus()` in the component body
Call `document.activeElement.focus()` in the body
Call it inside `useMemo` with no dependencies so it only ever runs once
questions.why: The node exists only after commit, so focus it in an effect (or let React's `autoFocus` do it on mount). In the body the ref is still `null` on the first render, and `useMemo` runs during render too, before the DOM exists.
questions.asked: Common small task; checks that you know where DOM work goes.

questions.q: Why does the React documentation say not to read or write `ref.current` during rendering (except for lazy initialisation)?
choices: It throws in development builds to catch memory leaks from long-lived refs
Refs are only created after the first render has finished
Rendering stops being predictable: React cannot see ref changes
It forces a second render each time a ref is read
questions.why: Render output should depend only on props, state and context. A ref changes silently, so output based on it can go stale or differ between renders React replays. Nothing throws and no renders are forced; it is a purity rule.
questions.asked: Checks the purity rules behind refs, which the React Compiler depends on.

questions.q: How often does this construct a `Parser`?
questions.code: const parser = useRef(new Parser(config));
choices: Once, on mount, exactly like a lazy `useState` initialiser
Only when `config` changes identity
Twice on mount, then never again
On every render, although only the first one is kept
questions.why: `new Parser(config)` is evaluated as an argument on every render; `useRef` just ignores it after mount. For expensive objects, start with `useRef(null)` and create lazily: `if (ref.current === null) ref.current = new Parser(config)`. `useRef` has no lazy-function form.
questions.asked: Checks that you do not assume `useRef` works like `useState(() => ...)`.

questions.q: In React 19, an inline ref callback with no cleanup return, `ref={(node) => log(node)}`, is on an element that re-renders. What does it log on each re-render?
choices: `null`, then the node, because the function identity changed
Nothing: ref callbacks run only on mount and unmount, never on re-render
The node twice, once for render and once for commit
Only the node, as React 19 ignores `null` calls
questions.why: A new inline function is a different ref, so React detaches the old one (calling it with `null`) and attaches the new one with the node. Usually harmless; if the callback is expensive, memoise it with `useCallback` or return a cleanup function in React 19.
questions.asked: Explains a confusing log pattern people see with inline ref callbacks.

questions.q: In React 19 development with `<StrictMode>`, a ref callback that returns a cleanup function mounts. What runs?
choices: Attach once; StrictMode does not affect refs
Cleanup first, then attach once
Attach twice, with no cleanup call between
Attach, cleanup, attach again
questions.why: React 19's StrictMode also simulates unmount and remount for ref callbacks, so a missing or wrong cleanup shows up in development. It mirrors what StrictMode does for effects. Production attaches once.
questions.asked: A React 19 detail; shows you know StrictMode checks refs now too.

questions.q: A list needs a DOM ref for each row so it can scroll any row into view. What is the usual approach?
choices: Call `useRef` inside the `map`, once per row
Give each row an `id` attribute and call `getElementById` at scroll time
Keep a `Map` in one ref and fill it from a ref callback per row
Store the row nodes in state as they mount, one by one
questions.why: Hooks cannot be called in a loop, so keep one ref holding a `Map` from id to node, set in each row's ref callback and removed in its cleanup. Querying by id works but bypasses React; storing nodes in state causes a render per row.
questions.asked: Tests refs, rules of hooks and ref callbacks together.

questions.q: A React 19 codebase still wraps components in `forwardRef`. What is true?
choices: It still works, but `ref` can now be read as a normal prop
It throws, as `forwardRef` was removed in React 19
It is required whenever a parent passes `ref` to a function component
It works only with class components in React 19
questions.why: React 19 passes `ref` to function components as a regular prop, so `forwardRef` is no longer needed, but it has not been removed; a codemod can migrate it. Class components have always received refs directly.
questions.asked: Migration knowledge; interviewers check you know the new default.

questions.q: Why expose `{ focus }` through `useImperativeHandle` rather than handing the parent the raw `<input>` node?
choices: Raw DOM nodes cannot be passed between components through props at all
It makes the input controlled, which the parent needs
It is faster, since the node is not serialised
A small API stops parents depending on or mutating internals
questions.why: Passing the node lets any parent change styles, values or listeners behind React's back. Exposing only `focus` keeps the component in charge of its DOM and lets you refactor the markup. Passing nodes is possible and cheap; it is an encapsulation choice.
questions.asked: Tests API design sense for imperative escape hatches.

questions.q: A component measures a panel with a `ResizeObserver`. What must the effect do?
choices: Nothing more, because observers stop by themselves when the node is removed
Call `ro.observe` again on every render to stay current
Return `() => ro.disconnect()` so the observer is released
Store `ro` in state so later renders can use it
questions.why: Observers, like listeners and timers, are external resources, and the effect must undo what it set up. `disconnect()` in the cleanup releases it on unmount and before re-runs. Observing again every render would stack observations.
questions.asked: Checks the setup/cleanup habit on a less familiar browser API.

questions.q: `value` goes 0, then 1, then 2. What does the component show after the last change?
choices: undefined
questions.why: Each render returns what the ref held before this render's effect updates it, so the render for 2 shows 1. It relies on reading a ref during render, which the React docs discourage; storing the previous value in state and comparing during render is the recommended version.
questions.asked: A well-known hook; knowing its caveat is what sets a strong answer apart.

questions.q: What does `useLayoutEffect` cost that `useEffect` does not?
choices: It runs twice per commit in production builds
It cannot read DOM refs, only measure them
It re-runs on every render, whatever its dependencies
It blocks the browser from painting until it finishes
questions.why: Layout effects run synchronously after DOM changes and before paint, so slow work there delays the frame the user sees. Use them only for measure-then-adjust cases; default to `useEffect`. They follow dependencies just like `useEffect`.
questions.asked: Knowing why it is not the default is the point of the question.

questions.q: What is wrong with this component?
choices: Nothing; the hook still runs whenever it is needed
`useState` must be passed `user` as its first argument
The hook is skipped on some renders, so the hook order can change
Early returns are not allowed at all in components that also use hooks
questions.why: React tracks hooks by call order. When `user` goes from missing to present, the number of hooks changes and React throws "Rendered more hooks than during the previous render". Call all hooks before any early return. Early returns themselves are fine.
questions.asked: The most common rules-of-hooks violation in real code.

questions.q: Each order row needs its own `useState`. A teammate calls `useState` inside `orders.map`. What is the fix?
choices: Extract an `OrderRow` component that calls `useState` itself
Keep it; the order of hooks stays stable if the list does
Use one `useState` per index, declared at the top of the file
Wrap the `map` in `useMemo` so the hooks are called once
questions.why: Hooks in a loop break as soon as the list length changes. Each row as its own component gets its own hook state, keyed by `key`. Alternatively keep one state object keyed by order id in the parent. `useMemo` does not make hooks legal inside it.
questions.asked: Shows you know the structural fix, not just the rule.

questions.q: Why does this fail?
questions.code:
<button onClick={() => {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  setOpen(true);
}}>Menu</button>
choices: State cannot be set inside arrow functions
`useState` needs an import alias before it can be used inside handlers
Event handlers must be declared with `function`
Hooks can only be called while React renders a component
questions.why: Hooks attach state to the component currently rendering. An event handler runs later, outside render, so React throws "Invalid hook call". Declare the state at the top of the component and call the setter in the handler.
questions.asked: Basic rule; shows whether you know what a hook is attached to.

questions.q: The lint rule flags `useFetch` being called inside `function loadUserData()`. What is the fix?
choices: Disable the rule for that line; the call is fine
Move `loadUserData` into a `useEffect` callback so it runs after render instead
Rename it `useUserData` (or call it from a component) so it is a hook
Mark `loadUserData` as `async` so hooks are allowed
questions.why: Hooks may only be called from components or other hooks, and the lint rule recognises hooks by the `use` prefix. Renaming makes the rules apply to its callers too. Calling hooks from inside an effect is itself a violation.
questions.asked: Checks you understand why the `use` naming convention exists.

questions.q: `useFormatPrice(amount)` just returns `Intl.NumberFormat(...).format(amount)` and calls no hooks. What should it be?
choices: Kept as is, since any reusable function in a React codebase counts as a hook
A component, since it produces something rendered
Wrapped in `useMemo` inside, to justify the name
A plain function `formatPrice`, so it can be called anywhere
questions.why: The `use` prefix tells readers and the linter that the function calls hooks, which restricts where it can be called. A pure helper should be a plain function, usable in loops, conditions and handlers. Adding a hook just to keep the name is backwards.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know what makes something a hook.

questions.q: Can you call `useState` inside a class component's `render` method?
choices: Yes, class components have supported hooks since React 16.8
Yes, but only outside of `render`
No, hooks work only in function components and hooks
Only when the class is wrapped with a `@hooks` decorator
questions.why: Hooks depend on the function-component render model. Classes keep using `this.state` and lifecycle methods. To reuse hook logic in a class, wrap the class in a small function component that calls the hook and passes values down.
questions.asked: Relevant when working in mixed legacy codebases.

questions.q: In React 19, which of these may be called inside an `if` block?
choices: `use`
`useContext`
`useState`
`useMemo`
questions.why: `use` (for promises and context) is designed to be called conditionally and in loops, although still only during render. All other hooks must be called unconditionally in the same order every render.
questions.asked: A React 19 exception to the rules; shows you are current.

questions.q: What do the two classic rules in `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` check?
choices: `rules-of-hooks` checks dependency arrays; `exhaustive-deps` checks naming
They check cleanups: one rule covers timers and the other covers event listeners and subscriptions
`rules-of-hooks` checks imports; `exhaustive-deps` checks unused state
`rules-of-hooks` checks where hooks are called; `exhaustive-deps` checks dependency arrays
questions.why: `rules-of-hooks` enforces top-level, unconditional calls from components and hooks; `exhaustive-deps` checks that effect and memo dependency arrays list every reactive value used. Neither checks cleanups. Newer versions add React Compiler rules alongside them.
questions.asked: Knowing the tooling that enforces the rules is expected of a mid-level dev.

questions.q: A teammate adds `// eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` above an effect that reads `filters`. What is the usual risk?
choices: The build fails in production because the rule is disabled
The effect runs on every render instead of when `filters` changes
The effect silently uses stale `filters` when they change
React ignores the dependency array on effects with comments
questions.why: Omitting a value the effect reads means React will not re-run it when that value changes, so it keeps working with old data. Fix the reason the dependency was unwanted: move objects inside, depend on primitives, or use `useEffectEvent` for non-reactive reads.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear "do not lie to the linter" and what to do instead.

questions.q: Why does this `useMemo` recompute on every render?
choices: `useMemo` only caches when the dependency array has one entry
`rows.map` returns a new array, which busts the cache
`format` is not listed as a dependency, so React skips caching
`opts` is a new object each render, so a dependency always differs
questions.why: Dependencies are compared with `Object.is`, and `opts` is re-created every render. List `locale` and `currency` instead, or build `opts` inside the memo callback. What the callback returns never affects whether it re-runs.
questions.asked: The same identity trap as effects, applied to memoisation.

questions.q: What is wrong with putting `analytics.track("viewed", id)` inside a `useMemo` callback so it runs only when `id` changes?
choices: It runs during render, may run twice or be discarded; use an effect
Nothing; `useMemo` is the cheapest place for one-off side effects
It never runs, because the callback's return value is `undefined`
It runs after paint, which is too late for analytics to be accurate at all
questions.why: `useMemo` runs during rendering, which must be pure: StrictMode calls it twice in development, and React may throw the cache away and recompute. Side effects that follow what is on screen belong in `useEffect`; ones caused by a click belong in the handler.
questions.asked: Checks you treat `useMemo` as a cache, not a lifecycle hook.

questions.q: The total shows the old tax rate after `taxRate` changes. Why?
choices: `useMemo` cannot read values that come from props, only values from state
Multiplications are cached by the JavaScript engine itself
`taxRate` is not a dependency, so the cached result is reused
The memo only updates after a second render has happened
questions.why: The callback re-runs only when a listed dependency changes, so a missing one leaves a stale value. The exhaustive-deps rule catches it. For arithmetic this cheap, drop the `useMemo` entirely and compute during render.
questions.asked: Stale memoised values are a quieter version of stale effects.

questions.q: In development with `<StrictMode>`, a `useMemo` callback logs twice on mount. Is that a bug?
choices: No: StrictMode calls it twice to check purity; production calls it once
Yes: the dependency array must contain an object that changes
Yes: `useMemo` should never run more than once per component
No: `useMemo` always runs twice, once for the render phase and once for the commit
questions.why: StrictMode double-invokes pure functions, including `useMemo` and `useState` initialisers, and keeps one result. A pure calculation does not care. It becomes a real bug only if the callback has side effects.
questions.asked: Tells apart dev-only checks from real problems.

questions.q: `Card` is wrapped in `memo`. Why does it still re-render each time `Page` does?
choices: `memo` only works for components that take no props
`children` is a new element object each render, so props differ
`memo` ignores parents that hold state of their own
The `<b>` tag forces a render every time, because it is a native DOM tag
questions.why: JSX creates new element objects every render, and `children` is just a prop, so the shallow comparison fails. Memoise the children element, move state down, or accept it; the React Compiler memoises such JSX for you.
questions.asked: The subtle reason many `memo` wrappers do nothing.

questions.q: A handler is only passed to a native `<button onClick>`. What does wrapping it in `useCallback` achieve?
choices: It stops the button from re-rendering on every parent render
It makes the click handler run faster when it is clicked
It prevents a memory leak from old handlers piling up
Almost nothing: DOM elements do not compare handler identity
questions.why: Stable identity only helps a consumer that compares it: a `memo` child or a hook dependency. A DOM element is updated by React either way, so this adds cost and noise for nothing. Old handlers are garbage-collected normally.
questions.asked: Tests the "when does useCallback matter" judgement.

questions.q: Why does the counter never change on screen when this reducer runs?
choices: Reducers must be `async` to update objects
`count` should be spread into a new variable first, then incremented
It returns the same object, so React bails out of the update
React ignores reducers that do not use a `switch`
questions.why: React compares the returned state to the previous one with `Object.is`. The same object means "no change", so React skips committing the update, even though the object was mutated. Return a new object: `{ ...state, count: state.count + 1 }`.
questions.asked: The reducer version of the mutation bug.

questions.q: What should a reducer's `default` case usually do for an unknown action type?
choices: Throw an error, so a typo in the type fails loudly
Return `undefined`, to signal that nothing happened
Call `dispatch` again with a safe fallback action
Reset the state to the initial value
questions.why: An unknown type is almost always a typo or a missing case, and throwing makes it obvious straight away. Returning `state` is also acceptable but hides the mistake. Returning `undefined` breaks the next render, and dispatching inside a reducer is not allowed.
questions.asked: Checks for defensive reducer design; TypeScript can make the check static.

questions.q: What does the third argument to `useReducer` do here?
questions.code: const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, userId, createInitialState);
choices: It is a middleware that runs before every dispatch
It is called again whenever `userId` changes, to reset the state to match
It replaces the reducer for the very first action that is dispatched
React calls `createInitialState(userId)` once to build the initial state
questions.why: It is the lazy-initialiser form: React calls the function with the second argument on mount only, so expensive setup does not run every render. Like `useState`, later changes to `userId` are ignored.
questions.asked: Tests knowledge of the full `useReducer` signature.

questions.q: What does the `console.log` print when `state.count` is 0?
choices: `undefined`
It depends on batching
questions.why: `dispatch` queues an update for the next render; `state` in this handler is the current render's snapshot. It works exactly like a `useState` setter. If you need the next state, call the reducer yourself: `reducer(state, action)`.
questions.asked: Checks the snapshot model carries over from `useState` to `useReducer`.

questions.q: Why is `fetch("/api/log", ...)` inside a reducer a mistake?
choices: Reducers must be pure; React may call them twice or replay them
Reducers run inside a web worker, so `fetch` is not defined there at all
The request is sent before the state changes, never after
It blocks the dispatch until the request completes
questions.why: React can call reducers more than once (StrictMode does it on purpose) and during rendering, so side effects there duplicate or happen at the wrong time. Do the request in the event handler that dispatches, or an effect.
questions.asked: The reducer purity rule, which also underlies Redux.

questions.q: Which set of action names follows the usual `useReducer` advice?
choices: `set_items`, `set_loading`, `set_error_message`
`item_added`, `item_removed`, `filter_changed`
`update`, `update2`, `update_all`
`setState`, `setPartialState`, `resetEverything`
questions.why: Actions should describe what happened, and the reducer decides what that means for state; one event can update several fields consistently. Setter-style actions push the logic back into components and make the reducer a pass-through.
questions.asked: A design question: separates reducers that model events from glorified setters.

questions.q: A reducer has a `switch` with no `default` case. A component dispatches `{ type: "rest" }` (a typo for `reset`). What happens?
choices: Nothing: unknown actions leave the state unchanged
React throws an "Unknown action" error before it calls the reducer
React logs a warning and falls back to the initial state
The state becomes `undefined`, and the next render likely crashes
questions.why: Falling off the end of the function returns `undefined`, which React stores as the new state. React does not validate actions. A `default` that throws (or returns `state`) avoids this.
questions.asked: Shows you know React treats the reducer's return value as gospel.

questions.q: An `increment` handler calls `dispatch({ type: "inc" })` twice in one click. The count starts at 0. What is it after the click?
choices: 2, since each call gets the latest state
1, because `state` is a snapshot
0, as dispatches are skipped in handlers
2 in development, 1 in production
questions.why: React queues both actions and runs the reducer on each in order, passing the result of one to the next, like the updater form of `setState`. The snapshot rule applies to reading `state` in the handler, not to how actions are processed.
questions.asked: Contrasts dispatch with `setCount(count + 1)`, which would give 1.

questions.q: What is a practical advantage of moving update logic from handlers into a reducer?
choices: Reducers make each component render less often
Reducers run on the server as well as in the browser, automatically
It can be unit-tested as a pure function, without rendering
Reducers skip StrictMode's development checks
questions.why: A reducer is `(state, action) => state`, so tests just call it with inputs and compare outputs. It does not change how often components render, and StrictMode checks it more, not less.
questions.asked: Testability is the answer interviewers look for beyond "it tidies code".

questions.q: A wizard managed by `useReducer` needs a "Start over" button. Which approach is cleanest?
choices: Call `window.location.reload()` from the click handler
Mutate `state` back to its defaults inside the handler
Call `useReducer` again inside the handler to reinitialise
Dispatch a `reset` action that returns the initial state
questions.why: A `reset` action keeps all state transitions in the reducer and reuses the same initial-state function. Remounting with a new `key` also works if the whole subtree should reset. Reloading loses unrelated state, mutation is a bug, and hooks cannot be called in handlers.
questions.asked: Checks idiomatic resets; mentioning the `key` alternative is a plus.

questions.q: In a TypeScript reducer over a union of actions, why do many codebases end the `switch` with this?
choices: Adding an action type without a case becomes a compile error
It makes the reducer run faster at runtime
It is required, or `useReducer` will refuse to accept the reducer
It stops React from calling the reducer twice
questions.why: If every union member is handled, `action` narrows to `never` in `default`. A new, unhandled member makes the assignment fail to compile, so the compiler lists every reducer that needs updating. The `throw` covers bad data at runtime.
questions.asked: Exhaustiveness checking is a strong TypeScript-in-React signal.

questions.q: What does `v` render here?
choices: `inner`
`undefined`
An error about nested providers
`outer`
questions.why: `useContext` reads the nearest provider above the calling component, not providers it renders itself. Here there is none, so it gets the default. A child inside the provider would see "inner".
questions.asked: A classic trick question about where context is read from.

questions.q: When should a custom hook return an array `[value, setValue]` rather than an object?
choices: Always, because arrays are faster to create than objects
Never, because arrays break the rules of hooks
When it returns two or so values callers usually rename
Only when the hook wraps `useState` directly
questions.why: Tuples make renaming free (`const [open, setOpen] = useToggle()`), which suits small `useState`-like hooks. With more than two or three values, positional returns get error-prone, and an object with named fields is clearer.
questions.asked: Hook API design; shows you think about the caller.

questions.q: `useFilters()` returns `{ filters, setFilter }` as a new object literal every render. A consumer's effect depends on the returned object. What happens?
choices: The effect re-runs every render, because the object is always new
The effect runs once, because the hook is called at the top level
React caches custom hook return values automatically
The effect never runs, as hook results are frozen
