questions.why: A new object has a new identity each render, so any dependency on it always changes. Consumers should depend on the fields they use, or the hook can memoise its return value with `useMemo`. React does not cache hook results.
questions.asked: Checks that you consider identity when designing a hook's return value.

questions.q: A `useCart` hook returns `addItem`, which a `memo` child uses. Why wrap `addItem` in `useCallback` inside the hook?
choices: Hooks may not return plain functions, only memoised ones
So its identity stays stable and the `memo` child can skip renders
So `addItem` can be called safely during render as well as in handlers
To prevent two components sharing the same cart
questions.why: Hooks are called from many places; returning stable callbacks means callers can pass them to memoised children or list them as dependencies without surprises. This is one of the few places `useCallback` pays off by default.
questions.asked: Tests where stable identity matters in library-style code.

questions.q: A `useFetch(url)` hook fetches inside an effect. What should the effect's dependency array be?
choices: `[]`, so the fetch runs once
`[useFetch]`
No array, so it always runs
`[url]`
questions.why: Hook parameters are reactive values like props, so the effect must re-run when `url` changes, or the hook keeps showing the first URL's data. With no array it would refetch on every render.
questions.asked: Tests that hook parameters are treated as dependencies.

questions.q: A component calls `useFetch(url, { headers: { Accept: "json" } })`, and the hook lists `options` in its effect's dependencies. What happens?
choices: It fetches once, since the header values themselves never change
It throws, since hooks cannot take object arguments
It refetches after every render, possibly in an endless loop
It fetches twice, once per key in `headers`
questions.why: The inline object is new each render, so the effect re-runs, sets state, re-renders, and fetches again. Design hook APIs to take primitives, read options through a ref, or require memoised objects, and say so in the docs.
questions.asked: A realistic infinite-loop bug; the fix shows API-design maturity.

questions.q: In a `useLocalStorage(key, initial)` hook, why read storage in a lazy initialiser `useState(() => read(key) ?? initial)`?
choices: It avoids reading and parsing storage on every render
Storage can only be read inside initialiser functions
It makes the value sync across browser tabs automatically
It lets the hook run safely during server rendering
questions.why: `localStorage` access and `JSON.parse` are synchronous and not free; the lazy form runs them once, on mount. Syncing tabs needs a `storage` event listener, and on the server `localStorage` does not exist, so the initialiser still needs a guard there.
questions.asked: A favourite take-home hook; details like this separate answers.

questions.q: `useDebouncedValue(query, 300)` sets a timer in an effect and clears it in cleanup. The user types "a", "ab", "abc" quickly. What does the hook return meanwhile?
choices: Each intermediate value, 300 ms after it was typed
An empty string until the user stops and presses the Enter key
"abc" immediately, then again after 300 ms
The last settled value, then "abc" 300 ms after typing stops
questions.why: Each keystroke re-runs the effect, and its cleanup cancels the previous timer, so only the last timer survives. Until then the hook keeps returning the old settled value. That is the whole debounce, built from effect cleanup.
questions.asked: Implementing this hook is a common live-coding task.

questions.q: A `useInterval(callback, delay)` hook stores `callback` in a ref and the interval calls `ref.current()`. Why not list `callback` in the interval effect's dependencies?
choices: Refs are required for any function that is passed to a browser timer
Intervals cannot call functions that come from props or from a hook caller
Callers pass a new function each render, which would restart the timer
The lint rule forbids functions in dependency arrays
questions.why: Inline callbacks change identity on every render, so depending on them would clear and restart the interval constantly. The ref keeps the latest callback while the effect depends only on `delay`. `useEffectEvent` now covers this pattern.
questions.asked: A well-known hook; explaining the ref shows real understanding of closures.

questions.q: Which `toggle` inside a `useToggle` hook stays correct when it is called twice in one event?
choices: `() => setOn(!on)`
`() => (ref.current = !ref.current)`
questions.why: The updater form reads the latest queued value, so two calls flip twice. `setOn(!on)` uses the render's snapshot, so two calls both set the same value. Reassigning a variable or a ref never tells React to re-render. Wrap the updater in `useCallback` with `[]` for a stable `toggle`.
questions.asked: Warm-up hook; checks the basics are right.

questions.q: How do you usually test a custom hook such as `useCounter` on its own?
choices: Call `useCounter()` directly at the top of the test file, like a function
Export its internal state and assert on the variables
Snapshot-test the hook's source code
Use `renderHook` from Testing Library and `act` around updates
questions.why: Hooks only work while React renders, so `renderHook` mounts a tiny test component and exposes `result.current`. Updates go in `act` so React processes them. Often testing through a real component that uses the hook is even better.
questions.asked: Checks practical testing knowledge for hooks.

questions.q: A `useModal()` hook returns a ready-made `<Modal>` element as well as `open`/`close`. What is the usual concern?
choices: It mixes rendering into a hook; a component API is usually clearer
Hooks are not allowed to create or return any JSX at all
The element leaks memory once it has been closed, since it is never unmounted
It breaks the rules of hooks for any hooks used inside the modal component
questions.why: Hooks are for reusable stateful logic; rendering belongs to components, where callers can compose and place it. Returning JSX hides where it renders and makes styling awkward. It is legal, just usually worse design.
questions.asked: Design judgement question: hooks versus components.

questions.q: What is wrong with this?
questions.code:
const useData = isAdmin ? useAdminData : useUserData;
const data = useData();
choices: Nothing, as long as both hooks call the same hooks inside
Hooks called through a variable skip React's hook tracking entirely, so nothing is stored
If `isAdmin` changes, a different hook runs with the other hook's state
The linter allows it, so it is safe in production
questions.why: React matches state to hook calls by position, not by name. Switching between two hooks while mounted feeds one hook's stored state to the other and breaks as soon as their internal hooks differ. Call both unconditionally, or split into two components.
questions.asked: A rules-of-hooks violation the linter may not catch.

questions.q: What does `useTransition` give you that importing `startTransition` from `react` does not?
choices: A way to mark updates as non-urgent
Automatic batching of the updates inside
Updates that skip rendering altogether
An `isPending` flag for showing progress
questions.why: Both mark updates inside as transitions. The hook version also returns `isPending`, which is true while the transition renders, so you can dim the old UI or show a spinner. The standalone function is for code outside components, such as a router.
questions.asked: Checks you know both forms and when each fits.

questions.q: A tab switch is wrapped in `startTransition` from `useTransition`. What is `isPending` usually used for?
choices: Blocking further clicks until the new tab has fully rendered on screen
Hinting that the switch is in progress while the old tab stays up
Deciding whether the nearest Suspense boundary shows its fallback
Cancelling the transition if the user clicks again
questions.why: During a transition React keeps showing the current UI, so `isPending` lets you add a subtle hint, such as dimming the tab bar. Nothing is blocked: a new click simply interrupts the old transition. Suspense fallbacks are not shown for content already on screen.
questions.asked: Practical use of the flag, not just its definition.

questions.q: Why should you not wrap `setText(e.target.value)` for a controlled input in `startTransition`?
choices: Transitions cannot be started from inside any event handler at all
Controlled inputs ignore every update made inside a transition
Input updates must be urgent, or typing lags behind the user
`startTransition` only accepts updates to objects or arrays
questions.why: Transition updates can be interrupted and delayed, but a controlled input must reflect each keystroke immediately. Keep the input update urgent and put the expensive part, such as filtering, in a transition or behind `useDeferredValue`.
questions.asked: The documented caveat that separates people who have used transitions.

questions.q: In React 19, what happens to `isPending` when you pass an async function to `startTransition`?
choices: It flips back to false as soon as the function starts running
It is always false, since async transitions are not allowed
It stays true forever unless you call `endTransition()` at the very end
It stays true until the promise settles and the updates render
questions.why: React 19 supports async functions ("Actions") in transitions and keeps `isPending` true for the whole async operation. This replaces hand-rolled `isSaving` state for many forms. There is no `endTransition` API.
questions.asked: A headline React 19 change to a hook you may already know.

questions.q: Inside an async transition, a `setPage(2)` call comes after an `await`. What caveat does the React documentation give?
choices: Updates after an `await` are urgent unless wrapped in `startTransition` again
State cannot be set after an `await` in any transition, so the call throws an error
Updates after an `await` are dropped when the component re-renders
The `await` cancels the transition, so `isPending` becomes false
questions.why: React loses track of the transition across the `await`, so later updates are treated as urgent, which can, for example, show a Suspense fallback. Wrapping them in another `startTransition` fixes it. The updates still apply.
questions.asked: A known sharp edge of async transitions.

questions.q: A `SearchResults` component receives `query` as a prop and renders slowly. Which hook fits, given you do not own the state setter?
choices: `useTransition`
`useDeferredValue`
`useLayoutEffect`
`useSyncExternalStore`
questions.why: `useDeferredValue(query)` lets the component render with a lagging copy of a value it receives, so the input stays responsive. `useTransition` needs access to the `setState` call. Layout effects and external stores do not address rendering priority.
questions.asked: Choosing between the two concurrent hooks is a common follow-up.

questions.q: In React 19, what does the second argument do in `useDeferredValue(query, "")`?
choices: It sets the delay, in milliseconds, before the deferred value is allowed to update
It is the fallback used if the deferred render throws an error
It is compared with `query` to decide whether to defer at all
It is rendered first, then React re-renders with `query` in the background
questions.why: The `initialValue` lets the first render show something cheap (such as empty results) and immediately schedule a background render with the real value. Without it, the first render uses `query` directly. There is no delay parameter; deferral is priority-based, not time-based.
questions.asked: Tests awareness of a React 19 addition to an existing hook.

questions.q: A page uses `useDeferredValue(query)` and passes it to `<Results query={deferred} />`, which is not memoised. Typing still lags. Why?
choices: `Results` still re-renders with its parent; wrap it in `memo`
The deferred value updates first, so the input waits for it
`useDeferredValue` only works together with a `<Suspense>` boundary
Deferred values are ignored in development builds, so it only lags in dev
questions.why: On the urgent render the deferred value is unchanged, but a non-memoised `Results` re-renders because its parent did. `memo` lets it skip that render, leaving the slow work to the background render with the new value.
questions.asked: The documented pitfall that makes `useDeferredValue` appear to do nothing.

questions.q: Why should `useId()` not be used for list keys?
choices: It returns numbers, and React requires keys to be strings
It is only available inside Server Components, not in lists
It identifies a component instance, not a data item
Its ids change every render, which remounts the list
questions.why: Keys must come from the data so React can match items across renders. `useId` gives one id per component instance, stable across renders but unrelated to which item is which. It is for accessibility attributes.
questions.asked: A common misuse; the answer shows you know what keys are for.

questions.q: A reusable `TextField` renders a `<label>` and an `<input>`. How should it link them when several fields appear on one page?
choices: Hard-code `id="field"` on every input, since ids are local to the component
Use `const id = useId()` for the input `id` and label `htmlFor`
Use `Math.random()` for the id on each render
Wrap the input in the label and give neither an id
questions.why: `useId` gives each instance a unique, render-stable id, which also matches between server and client. Hard-coded ids collide and `Math.random()` changes every render and breaks hydration. Wrapping works for the label, but not for `aria-describedby` hints.
questions.asked: The main use of `useId`; accessible forms are a common topic.

questions.q: Why does `useId` exist, instead of just using an incrementing module counter?
choices: A counter can differ between server and client, breaking hydration
Counters overflow after a few thousand components have mounted
Module-level variables are not allowed anywhere in React components
Counters re-run every render, so ids would change
questions.why: With server rendering, a global counter depends on the order components happen to render in, which may differ on the client, so ids mismatch. `useId` derives the id from the component's position in the tree, which is the same in both places.
questions.asked: Checks you know the hydration problem it solves.

questions.q: A form component needs ids for an email input, its hint and its error. What is the recommended way?
choices: Call `useId()` three times inside a loop over the field names
Call `useId()` once and add random numbers to it
One `useId()`, suffixed: `${id}-email`, `${id}-hint`
Use the field names directly as the ids on each element
questions.why: One `useId` per component plus fixed suffixes gives unique, related ids and avoids calling hooks in loops. Bare field names collide when the form appears twice, and random parts break rendering stability.
questions.asked: Small detail that shows you have used the hook in real forms.

questions.q: Two separate React roots on one page both use `useId`, and their ids collide. What fixes it?
choices: Give each root a different `identifierPrefix` option
Wrap each root in its own separate `<StrictMode>` component
Call `useId` with a different seed in each root
Render the second root inside a portal attached to the first
questions.why: Ids are unique within one root. `createRoot(el, { identifierPrefix: "cart-" })` (and the matching option on `hydrateRoot` and the server) namespaces each root's ids. `useId` takes no arguments.
questions.asked: Relevant for micro-frontends and widgets embedded in other pages.

questions.q: Which is a good fit for `useSyncExternalStore`?
choices: Fetching and caching a paginated list of orders from a REST API
Keeping a large form's input values between renders of the page
Deriving a filtered list from props during render
Reading `navigator.onLine` and following `online`/`offline` events
questions.why: It subscribes a component to a value that lives outside React and can change at any time, like browser state or a store library, without tearing during concurrent rendering. Fetching belongs in a data library; form values and derived data are ordinary state and computation.
questions.asked: Recognising its use cases is more important than its signature.

questions.q: Why should the `subscribe` function passed to `useSyncExternalStore` be declared outside the component (or be memoised)?
choices: Otherwise React throws, because store functions must be pure and module-level
A new function each render makes React resubscribe every render
Otherwise `getSnapshot` is never called on the server
Inline functions cannot call `addEventListener`
questions.why: React treats a different `subscribe` function as a new subscription, so it unsubscribes and subscribes again after each render. That works but wastes effort. Declaring it at module level (or with `useCallback`) keeps one subscription.
questions.asked: The main performance gotcha of the hook.

questions.q: What happens with this `getSnapshot`?
choices: It works fine, because React compares the snapshots field by field
It returns `undefined` because objects are not allowed
React warns it must be cached, then loops until "Maximum update depth"
It works, but re-subscribes to the store every time the store changes
questions.why: `getSnapshot` must return the same value when nothing changed, compared with `Object.is`. A new object each call looks like constant change, so React re-renders in a loop. Return a cached object from the store, or select primitives.
questions.asked: The number-one bug people hit when first using the hook.

questions.q: What is the optional third argument of `useSyncExternalStore`, `getServerSnapshot`, for?
choices: Fetching the store's initial value from your own API server at start-up
Replacing `getSnapshot` whenever the page detects it is offline
Logging snapshots to the server for debugging
Supplying the value for server rendering and hydration
questions.why: Stores like `window` sizes do not exist on the server, so this function returns what the server rendered, and the client uses it during hydration to avoid a mismatch before switching to `getSnapshot`. Omitting it makes server rendering of that component throw.
questions.asked: Shows depth on how external stores meet server rendering.

questions.q: In React 19.2, an effect calls `onVisit(url)`, created with `useEffectEvent`. Should `onVisit` go in the effect's dependency array?
choices: Yes, all functions used by an effect must be listed
No: effect events are not reactive, so they stay out of the list
Yes, but only in the case where `onVisit` reads some state value
No, because functions are compared by name, not identity
questions.why: An effect event always sees the latest props and state but is deliberately not a dependency, so reading `cartCount` inside it does not re-run the effect. The exhaustive-deps rule knows this. Functions are compared by identity, not name.
questions.asked: Checks understanding of what makes effect events different.

questions.q: Where may a function created by `useEffectEvent` be called?
choices: Anywhere, including render and child components
Only from event handlers such as `onClick`
Only from inside effects in the same component
Only from other hooks, not from components
questions.why: Effect events are for the non-reactive parts of effects. Calling them during render or passing them to other components is disallowed, and the lint rule reports it. For click handlers you just write a normal function.
questions.asked: Tests the constraints, which people forget once they like the hook.

questions.q: A chat effect connects to `roomId` and shows a notification styled with the current `theme` when connected. Which value belongs in `useEffectEvent`?
choices: `roomId`, so the effect does not reconnect
Both, so the effect never needs dependencies
Neither of them; list both as normal effect dependencies
`theme`, so the notification reads it without a reconnect
questions.why: Changing the room should reconnect, so `roomId` stays reactive. Changing the theme should not reconnect, so the notification logic that reads `theme` moves into an effect event. Listing `theme` would tear down the connection for a cosmetic change.
questions.asked: The exact example from the React docs; applying it shows real understanding.

questions.q: Why does `const user = use(fetch(url).then((r) => r.json()))` in a client component keep suspending?
choices: Each render creates a new promise, so it never settles for that render
`use` only accepts context, not promises, on the client
`fetch` is blocked inside client components by React 19 for safety reasons
The response must be awaited before `use` can read it
questions.why: `use` suspends until the promise it is given resolves, then re-renders, which creates a brand new promise, and so on. The promise must be cached or created outside render: by a Server Component, a loader, or a data library.
questions.asked: The main pitfall of `use` with promises.

questions.q: In React 19, can `use(ThemeContext)` appear after an early `return`?
choices: No, like all hooks it must come before any return
Only when `ThemeContext` was created with a default value
Yes: `use` may be called conditionally, unlike `useContext`
Only inside Server Components, where hooks are relaxed
questions.why: `use` is exempt from the "top level only" rule and can be called in conditions and loops during render. Swapping `use` in for `useContext` here is fine. Its other rule still holds: only call it while rendering.
questions.asked: Checks the one flexible hook in React 19.

questions.q: What arguments does the action passed to `useActionState` receive when the form is submitted?
questions.code:
const [state, formAction] = useActionState(saveProfile, { error: null });
<form action={formAction}>...</form>
choices: Only `formData`, like a plain form action
The submit event, then the previous state
The `FormData`, then a `dispatch` function
The previous state, then the `FormData`
questions.why: Wrapping an action in `useActionState` adds the previous state as the first argument, and whatever it returns becomes the next `state`. That makes it natural to return validation errors. Forgetting the extra parameter is a frequent bug when adopting it.
questions.asked: The signature change is the thing people get wrong.

questions.q: What does `useActionState` return?
choices: `[state, setState]`, like `useState`
`[state, formAction, isPending]`
`{ data, error, loading }`
`[formAction, isPending]`
questions.why: It returns the latest state produced by the action, a wrapped action to pass to a form or button, and a pending flag. There is no direct setter: state only changes through the action.
questions.asked: Basic React 19 API recall.

questions.q: Why does `pending` stay `false` while this form submits?
choices: `useFormStatus` only works with `onSubmit` handlers, not with the `action` prop
`pending` updates only after the action has resolved
It reads a parent form's status; this component owns the form
The button needs `type="submit"` to report status
questions.why: `useFormStatus` reads the nearest `<form>` above the component, like context. Here the form is rendered by the same component, so there is none above it. Move the button into a `SubmitButton` child rendered inside the form.
questions.asked: The most common `useFormStatus` bug.

questions.q: A user submits a `useActionState` form three times quickly. How does React run the three actions?
choices: In parallel, and whichever result arrives fastest wins
Only the last one; the earlier submits are cancelled by React
Only the first one; later submits are ignored until it ends
One after another, each receiving the previous result as state
questions.why: Actions from `useActionState` are queued and run sequentially, so each sees the state the previous one returned. That keeps state consistent but means slow actions add up; disable the button with `isPending` if repeats make no sense.
questions.asked: Deeper behaviour that matters for double submits.

questions.q: What does the second argument do in `useOptimistic(messages, (current, sent) => [...current, sent])`?
choices: It merges an optimistic value into the current state
It sends the message to the server optimistically, before the action
It reverts the list automatically if the server call fails
It compares old and new lists to decide on re-renders
questions.why: With the reducer form, `addOptimistic(msg)` calls it to produce the optimistic list shown while the action runs. When the action finishes, React drops the optimistic value and shows the real `messages` again. It does no networking and has no special failure logic.
questions.asked: Tests how the optimistic value is derived from real state.

questions.q: A click handler calls `setOptimisticLikes(n + 1)` without any action or transition. What happens?
choices: The optimistic value shows until the next unrelated render happens
It behaves exactly like a normal `setState` call would
React warns it is outside a transition, and it reverts
It is queued until the next form action runs
questions.why: Optimistic state only exists while an action or transition is pending. Outside one, React warns "An optimistic state update occurred outside a transition or action" and the value reverts immediately. Call it inside `startTransition` or a form action.
questions.asked: Shows you know optimistic state is tied to a pending action.

questions.q: What does `useDebugValue(isOnline ? "Online" : "Offline")` inside a custom hook do?
choices: Logs the value to the console on every render
Throws in production builds if the value passed is falsy
Adds a `data-debug` attribute to the DOM
Shows the label next to the hook in React DevTools
questions.why: It is purely for React DevTools, labelling custom hooks so you can inspect them. It has no runtime effect, and it is worth using mainly in shared library hooks. An optional formatter argument defers expensive formatting until inspected.
questions.asked: A niche hook; knowing it exists is enough.

questions.q: In a function component, what is the equivalent of a class's `componentDidMount` for starting a subscription?
choices: `useState` with a lazy initialiser
`useEffect` with an empty array
`useMemo` with an empty array
`useLayoutEffect` with no array
questions.why: An effect with `[]` runs after the first commit, like `componentDidMount`, and its cleanup plays the role of `componentWillUnmount`. Initialisers and memos run during render, and an effect with no array runs after every render.
questions.asked: Migration question; better answers add that effects are about sync, not lifecycle.

questions.q: Which hook feature replaces `componentWillUnmount`?
choices: A `useRef` flag that is checked during every render
The cleanup function returned from an effect
A `useState` setter called with `null`
The second argument passed to `useCallback`, when it is empty
questions.why: An effect's returned function runs before the effect re-runs and when the component unmounts. With `[]` it runs only on unmount, like `componentWillUnmount`. Refs and setters do not run code at unmount.
questions.asked: Basic lifecycle mapping for people coming from class code.

questions.q: What is the function-component counterpart to `shouldComponentUpdate` returning `false` for equal props?
choices: `useEffect` returning `false` after the first render
`useMemo` wrapped around the whole JSX return value
A `useRef` holding the last props, compared in render
`React.memo`, which compares props shallowly
questions.why: `memo` wraps a component and skips re-rendering when every prop is `Object.is`-equal (or your comparator says so). It is a performance hint, not a guarantee. Effects run after rendering, so they cannot stop one.
questions.asked: Migration knowledge; strong answers mention shallow comparison.

questions.q: A legacy integration needs the equivalent of `this.forceUpdate()` in a function component. What is the usual idiom?
choices: A reducer that always returns a new value, like `(x) => x + 1`
Call the component function again directly from inside itself
Write to a ref and read it during render to pick up the change
Call `root.render()` from inside the component on each change
questions.why: Dispatching an update that changes state guarantees a re-render. It is an escape hatch for data outside React; in most cases the real fix is to put that data in state or read it with `useSyncExternalStore`.
questions.asked: Tests knowledge of escape hatches and why they are a smell.

questions.q: What problem were hooks introduced (React 16.8) to solve?
choices: Function components were much slower to render than classes
Class components could not be rendered on the server at all
Sharing stateful logic without wrappers like HOCs
JSX could not be used inside class component render methods
questions.why: Before hooks, sharing stateful logic meant higher-order components or render props, which nest wrappers and hide data flow. Hooks let a function own state and effects and share them through custom hooks. Classes rendered fine on the server and with JSX.
questions.asked: A context question that shows you know why the API looks the way it does.

questions.q: What does `useRef(0)` return?
choices: The number 0 itself, frozen after the first render
A getter function that returns the current value
An object `{ current: 0 }`, the same object each time
A brand new `{ current: 0 }` object on every render
questions.why: React creates the ref object once and hands back the same object on every render, so changes to `current` persist. That stable identity is why refs can hold timers, DOM nodes and latest values.
questions.asked: Basic API recall that underpins every ref question.

questions.q: What is `useContext` for?
choices: Creating a new context object for the component tree it is called in
Storing state that survives the component being unmounted
Sharing a single `useState` between two sibling components automatically, without a parent
Reading the nearest matching provider's value above the component
questions.why: It subscribes the component to a context created with `createContext`, returning the nearest provider's value and re-rendering when it changes. `createContext` makes the context; the state itself still lives in whichever component renders the provider.
questions.asked: Warm-up; the follow-up is usually about re-render cost.

questions.q: A component sorts 20,000 rows, and it re-renders often for unrelated reasons. Which hook caches the sorted result between renders?
choices: `useMemo`
`useRef`
`useCallback`
`useEffect`
questions.why: `useMemo(() => sortRows(rows), [rows])` keeps the result until `rows` changes. `useCallback` caches a function, not its result, and sorting in an effect would need extra state and an extra render.
questions.asked: Choosing the right hook for the job.

questions.q: Which dependency array makes an effect run only after the first render?
choices: No array at all
`[null]`
`[true]`
questions.why: An empty array means "no reactive values", so the effect never needs to re-run after mount (StrictMode adds one extra dev run). Omitting the array runs it after every render. Constant values like `[true]` also never change, but they are just noise.
questions.asked: Basic, but the StrictMode caveat shows depth.

questions.q: What does `useReducer(reducer, initialState)` return?
choices: `[state, setState]`
`{ state, actions }`
`[dispatch, state]`
`[state, dispatch]`
questions.why: You read `state` and call `dispatch(action)`; React runs `reducer(state, action)` to get the next state. There is no direct setter, which is what keeps all transitions inside the reducer.
questions.asked: Quick API recall; the follow-up is usually why there is no direct setter.

questions.q: An effect reads `status` and `page`. When should it re-run?
choices: When `status` or `page` changes: `[status, page]`
Only when `page` changes, since `status` is just a filter
After every render, just to be safe about it
Only on mount; refetch by hand after changes
questions.why: Every reactive value the effect reads is a dependency, and React re-runs the effect when any of them change. The lint rule will suggest exactly `[status, page]`. Running after every render wastes work.
questions.asked: Checks the core rule for dependency arrays.

questions.q: Is it safe to pass `setCount` straight down to a child as a prop?
choices: No, setters only work in the component that declared them
Only if the child is wrapped in `memo` first
Yes: the setter is stable and updates the parent's state
Only after wrapping it in `useCallback` in the parent
questions.why: Setters keep the same identity for the component's lifetime and always update the owner's state. Often a named callback such as `onIncrement` is a clearer API, but the setter itself works and needs no memoising.
questions.asked: Tests understanding of where state lives.

questions.q: What does `useCallback(fn, deps)` do?
choices: Runs `fn` once and caches whatever result it returns
Makes `fn` run asynchronously, after the render commits
Prevents `fn` from ever reading stale state or props
Returns the same function until a dependency changes
questions.why: It caches the function itself, so its identity is stable for `memo` children and dependency arrays. It does not call the function (that is `useMemo`) and it can make stale closures worse if deps are missing.
questions.asked: Definition question; the stale-closure caveat is the bonus point.

questions.q: A component subscribes to a WebSocket and also syncs `document.title`. How many effects should it have?
choices: Two: one per concern, each with its own dependencies
One, since a component should only ever have a single effect
None: both of these belong in event handlers instead
One per render, created inside a loop over the concerns
questions.why: Split effects by what they synchronise. Separate effects get separate dependency lists and cleanups, so a title change does not reconnect the socket. There is no limit on how many effects a component has.
questions.asked: Code organisation with effects; shows sync-based thinking.

questions.q: A component declares effect A, then effect B. In what order do they run after a render?
choices: B, then A, in reverse declaration order
In parallel, on separate microtasks
A, then B, in declaration order
Random, depending on scheduling
questions.why: Within a component, effects (and their cleanups) run in the order they are declared. Across components, children's effects run before their parent's.
questions.asked: A small fact that comes up when effects depend on each other.

questions.q: Which combination builds a clock that ticks every second and stops cleanly on unmount?
choices: `useRef` for the time, and a `setInterval` started directly in the component body on render
`useMemo` that starts the interval and `useState` for the time
`useState` for the time and `setInterval` inside the click handler only
`useState` for the time, and an effect with `setInterval` plus a clearing cleanup
questions.why: The time must be state so the screen updates, and the interval is an external resource started in an effect and cleared in its cleanup. Starting it in the body starts a new interval each render; a ref would not re-render.
questions.asked: A small classic component that exercises the core hooks.

questions.q: In `const [items, setItems] = useState([])`, where do the names `items` and `setItems` come from?
choices: You choose them: array destructuring names both parts
React requires the `set` prefix to recognise setters
They must match a key that exists in the initial state object
The linter generates them from the initial value
questions.why: `useState` returns a two-element array and destructuring lets you name each part. The `[thing, setThing]` convention is only a convention. This is why hooks return arrays rather than objects with fixed names.
questions.asked: Basic, but checks you know it is just array destructuring.

questions.q: When does a `useEffect` callback run relative to rendering?
choices: During render, just before the component returns its JSX
Before the component function is called for that render
After React commits the DOM, usually after paint
Only when the user interacts with the component
questions.why: Rendering computes JSX, React commits changes to the DOM, and then effects run, typically after the browser has painted. That is why effects can read the DOM but should not be used for values needed in the first frame.
questions.asked: The timing model behind most effect questions.

questions.q: When is `setCount(count + 1)` perfectly fine?
choices: Never; you should always use the updater form instead
Only inside effects, and never inside event handlers
Only when `count` is also mirrored in a ref for safety
One update per event, with no stale callback involved
questions.why: In a plain click handler that updates once, `count` is the current render's value and the result is correct. The updater form is needed when you queue several updates or the code runs later from an old closure, such as a timer.
questions.asked: Avoids the cargo-cult "always use the updater" answer.

questions.q: A modal's open/closed flag is only used by the page that renders it. Which hook fits?
choices: `useState`
`useRef`
`useContext`
`useMemo`
questions.why: The flag changes and the screen must update, so it is state, colocated in the page. A ref would not re-render, context is for values many distant components need, and `useMemo` caches derived values.
questions.asked: Choosing the simplest tool that works.

questions.q: Dependencies are unchanged since the last render. What does `useMemo` return?
choices: `undefined`, until the dependencies change again
The cached value from an earlier render
A new value, from calling the function again
A promise that resolves to the cached value
questions.why: With equal dependencies React reuses the stored result instead of calling your function. React may occasionally throw the cache away, so the code must still be correct if it recalculates.
questions.asked: Checks the basic contract and its caveat.

questions.q: Which should you reach for by default when you need an effect?
choices: `useLayoutEffect`, to be safe with layout
`useInsertionEffect`, the newest of the three
`useEffect`, unless measuring before paint
Whichever effect hook runs first in the tree
questions.why: `useEffect` does not block painting, so it is the default. Switch to `useLayoutEffect` only for measure-then-adjust work that would otherwise flicker. `useInsertionEffect` is for CSS-in-JS libraries.
questions.asked: Tests sensible defaults.

questions.q: Can a custom hook call other custom hooks?
choices: No, only built-in hooks may be called
Only one level deep, then it breaks
Only if both hooks share their state
Yes, hooks compose like functions
questions.why: A custom hook is just a function that calls hooks, and those can be built-in or custom. Each call still gets its own state. Composition is the main reason hooks replaced HOCs.
questions.asked: Basic composition knowledge.

questions.q: An effect runs an async function that may reject. Where should the error be handled?
choices: Inside `load` with `try/catch`, setting error state
React catches it and shows the nearest error boundary
In the cleanup function returned by the effect
Nowhere; rejected promises in effects are ignored
questions.why: Error boundaries only catch errors thrown during rendering, not rejections from async code in effects. Without a `try/catch` you get an unhandled rejection and the UI stays in its loading state. Set an error state, or rethrow it via state to reach a boundary.
questions.asked: Async errors in effects are a frequent gap in candidates' code.

questions.q: `handleChange` is wrapped in `useCallback` with `[form]` as its dependency and passed to 30 memoised fields. Why do all fields re-render on every keystroke?
choices: `memo` ignores function props, so it never helps with callbacks
The fields re-render because they are controlled inputs
`form` changes on each keystroke, so the callback is new each time
`useCallback` only stabilises functions with no parameters
questions.why: A callback that depends on state changes whenever that state does. Using the updater form, `setForm((f) => ({ ...f, [name]: value }))`, removes `form` from the deps and keeps the identity stable.
questions.asked: Shows how updater functions help memoisation, not just correctness.

questions.q: One click sets both `page` and `pageSize`, and an effect depends on `[page, pageSize]`. How many times does it fetch?
choices: Twice, once for each dependency change
Zero, as the two changes cancel out
Three times, including one automatic retry
Once, as both updates render together
questions.why: Both updates are batched into one render, and effects run once per commit, comparing the whole dependency array. So the effect sees both changes at once and runs a single time.
questions.asked: Connects batching and effect runs.

questions.q: `const [total] = useState(() => sum(items))` shows the wrong total after `items` changes. Why, and what is the fix?
choices: State is set once; compute `sum(items)` during render
The initialiser is async; await it before rendering
The array is compared deeply; pass a copy of `items` instead
Lazy initialisers are skipped in production builds; call `sum` directly instead
questions.why: Copying derived data into state freezes it at the first value. A value computed from props or other state should be calculated during render, cached with `useMemo` only if it is expensive.
questions.asked: The derived-state mistake in its hooks form.

questions.q: A component calls `useFetch(url)`, which keeps `data` in state. When `url` changes, what does the screen show until the new response arrives?
choices: Nothing, because the hook's state resets for a new URL
A Suspense fallback, as React suspends automatically
The previous URL's data, unless the hook clears it
An error, because `data` no longer matches `url`
questions.why: Hook state belongs to the component and persists across renders; a changed argument does not reset it. The hook should reset `data` or track which URL it belongs to, or the caller can remount with `key={url}`. Query libraries handle this with keyed caches.
questions.asked: A subtle stale-data bug in hand-rolled fetching hooks.

questions.q: A `useLayoutEffect` measures a node and calls `setHeight(h)`. When does that re-render happen?
choices: After the browser paints, like any other update
On the next user interaction
Only in development builds
Synchronously, before the browser paints
questions.why: Updates inside layout effects are processed synchronously before paint, so the user never sees the unmeasured frame. That is the point of the hook, and also why heavy work there hurts responsiveness.
questions.asked: Explains how layout effects avoid flicker.

questions.q: A component suspends on its very first render, before it ever mounted. What happens to the state its `useState` initialiser created?
choices: It is thrown away; React starts again on retry
It is kept, and reused once the data finally arrives
It is saved in the nearest Suspense boundary for later
It is copied into the fallback component
questions.why: React does not keep state for trees that suspended before mounting, so initialisers and refs are created again on the retry. Anything expensive or identity-sensitive should be cached outside the suspending component.
questions.asked: A deep Suspense detail that explains surprising re-initialisation.

questions.q: Content is already visible. A navigation in `startTransition` makes a child suspend. What does the user see?
choices: The nearest Suspense fallback straight away
The old content stays until the new content is ready
A blank screen until the data for the child has resolved
An error, because transitions are not allowed to suspend
questions.why: Transitions avoid replacing visible content with fallbacks: React keeps the old UI (with `isPending` true) and switches when ready. Without a transition, the same suspension would show the fallback.
questions.asked: Shows how transitions and Suspense work together in routing.

questions.q: A store read with `useSyncExternalStore` is mutated inside a `startTransition`. What does React do with that update?
choices: Treats it as a non-blocking transition like any other update
Ignores it until the transition that caused it has finished
Renders it urgently: external stores cannot be transitions
Throws, because stores cannot change during transitions
questions.why: External stores have only one current value, so React cannot keep an old and new version side by side. It de-opts to a synchronous render, which can show Suspense fallbacks. State owned by React (useState/useReducer) is what transitions work best with.
questions.asked: Explains a trade-off of external store libraries in concurrent React.

questions.q: What is the third argument of `useImperativeHandle(ref, create, deps)` for?
choices: The initial value of the ref before mount
The list of methods the parent is allowed to call
A cleanup function that React calls when the component unmounts
When to recreate the handle, like memo dependencies
questions.why: React calls `create` again only when a dependency changes, so the parent keeps the same handle object otherwise. Without it, the handle is recreated after every render. The exposed methods are whatever `create` returns.
questions.asked: Rarely used detail; tests reading the API carefully.
